nameStory: The striped hairstreak gets its name from the distinctive striped pattern on the undersides of its wings, which look like delicate pencil lines drawn across gray-brown paper. The 'hairstreak' part comes from the thin, hair-like tails that extend from the hindwings, a signature feature of this butterfly family that makes them look like they have tiny streamers attached.
description: The striped hairstreak is a small, delicate butterfly that belongs to the gossamer-winged butterfly family, known for their soft, shimmery wing scales. These butterflies are compact and dainty, typically spanning about an inch across when their wings are open. The upper sides of their wings are a plain grayish-brown, but flip them over and you'll see the beautiful striped pattern that gives them their name. Like other hairstreaks, they have small, thread-like tails on their hindwings that help confuse predators about which end is the head.

idTips.label: Wing stripes
idTips.description: Look for clean, parallel white and dark stripes running across the underside of both wings, creating a distinctive banded pattern that feels almost geometric when you see it up close

idTips.label: Wing tails
idTips.description: Two thin, hair-like projections extend from each hindwing like delicate streamers that flutter in even the slightest breeze

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Small and compact, about the size of a quarter when wings are spread, with a quick, darting flight pattern that makes them seem to vanish and reappear

idTips.label: Upper wing color
idTips.description: Plain gray-brown upper wings that look almost dusty or weathered, completely different from the patterned undersides

idTips.label: Orange spots
idTips.description: Small orange or reddish spots near the wing tails on the underside, often accompanied by metallic blue scales that catch the light

habitat: Striped hairstreaks prefer woodland edges, clearings, and areas where forests meet open spaces throughout New England's mixed deciduous and coniferous forests. You'll often spot them in sunny gaps within wooded areas, along hiking trails, or in forest clearings where wildflowers bloom. They're particularly drawn to areas with their host plants - various trees and shrubs in the rose family, including wild cherry and plum trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically May, when you might catch them nectaring on early wildflowers in woodland clearings. Look for their quick, erratic flight patterns among blooming trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in early to mid-summer (June-July) when adults are most abundant and actively mating. This is the best time to observe their distinctive striped underwing pattern as they pause to feed on flowers or rest on leaves.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by late summer, with most adults finishing their lifecycle by early fall. Eggs overwinter on host plant twigs, invisible to casual observers.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - eggs remain dormant on tree branches throughout the cold months, waiting for spring warmth to trigger hatching.

funFact: Striped hairstreaks are master tricksters - those tail-like projections on their hindwings aren't just for show, they actually mimic antennae and work with eye spots to make predators think the butterfly's rear end is its head, causing birds to attack the wrong end and giving the butterfly a chance to escape with just damaged wing tips instead of a fatal head injury!
confusionNotes: The striped hairstreak can be tricky to distinguish from its cousin, the banded hairstreak, since both have striped underwings. Remember this: striped hairstreaks have cleaner, more parallel lines that run straight across the wing like ruled paper, while banded hairstreaks have more irregular, jagged bands that look more like a broken fence.
contextualKnowledge: The striped hairstreak belongs to a confusing group of look-alike butterflies that even experienced naturalists find challenging. New England is home to six different hairstreak species in the same genus, and they're often called 'the hairstreak complex' because telling them apart requires close examination of wing patterns and sometimes even microscopic features.
compareHints: Among New England's hairstreaks, the striped hairstreak stands out for having the most regular, parallel striping pattern - think of neat ruled lines rather than the zigzag or broken patterns of banded or Edwards' hairstreaks. Unlike the coral hairstreak which lacks tails entirely, or the hickory hairstreak with its distinctive white patches, the striped hairstreak maintains that classic 'lined notebook paper' appearance on its underwings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its hairstreak relatives, the Banded Hairstreak is distinguished by its prominent white-edged bands across both wings, while Edwards' Hairstreak has more muted markings and Coral Hairstreak lacks tails entirely.
Among the hairstreaks in its genus, Edwards' Hairstreak is most similar to Banded Hairstreak, but Edwards' has more subdued underside markings and is more closely associated with scrub oak habitats.
Among New England's hairstreaks, the coral hairstreak stands out for what it lacks - no white stripes like the banded or striped hairstreaks, and no blue patches like some others.
Among New England's hairstreaks, the Hickory Hairstreak is most similar to the Banded Hairstreak, but Banded Hairstreaks typically have more distinct banding patterns on their underwings.
Among its hairstreak relatives, the Acadian stands out for its very short upper tail and relatively plain gray underside.
